metadata.title: Low-Frequency Ground Penetrating Radar (GPR) Dataset Acquired via Ground-Based and UAV Platforms
metadata.description:
This dataset provides a curated collection of low-frequency Ground Penetrating Radar (GPR) data acquired within a joint research initiative involving the Istituto Nazionale di Geofisica e Vulcanologia (INGV) and the Università degli Studi di Salerno (UNISA). The dataset has been specifically designed to enable comparative studies between conventional ground-based GPR acquisition and innovative UAV-mounted GPR sensing.

The acquisition campaign was jointly planned and executed by INGV and UNISA, combining geophysical expertise, field survey experience, and advanced data engineering methodologies. INGV contributed its long-standing expertise in geophysical surveying, site selection, and field deployment strategies, ensuring scientifically rigorous acquisition protocols. UNISA contributed to system integration, UAV-based sensing configuration, data synchronization, georeferencing, and the design of data processing pipelines.

Data were acquired in two distinct modalities:

  1. Ground-based cart acquisition – The GPR antenna was mounted on a manually operated cart. This configuration ensures high data quality, stable antenna-ground coupling, and minimal acquisition artifacts. However, it requires significant human effort and favorable ground conditions.

  2. UAV-based acquisition – The same GPR antenna was mounted on an Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV). This approach enables rapid deployment with minimal human intervention and is particularly suitable for hazardous or post-disaster environments where direct ground access may be unsafe. Due to the air–ground interface and UAV motion/control imperfections, this modality introduces noise and artifacts, resulting in lower signal quality compared to the ground-based configuration.

Importantly, both acquisition modalities use the same antenna system and GPS positioning framework, ensuring spatial consistency and enabling rigorous comparative analysis. This design allows researchers to investigate:

  • Signal degradation mechanisms due to aerial deployment

  • Pre-processing and denoising strategies

  • Enhancement and artifact mitigation techniques

  • Information extraction and subsurface feature detection pipelines

  • Domain adaptation approaches between acquisition modalities

The survey was initially carried out using a ground-coupled GPR system mounted on a cart, employing the same antenna and acquisition configuration later used for the airborne measurements. These preliminary acquisitions allowed the identification of the main subsurface features and provided a reference dataset for subsequent UAV-based investigations.

Based on these results, the UAV mission was accurately planned to replicate the same survey lines, ensuring spatial consistency between datasets. The UAV-borne survey was therefore conducted along the same transects acquired with the cart-based system, with trajectory control ensured by high-precision GNSS positioning in Real-Time Kinematik (RTK) mode, enabling centimeter-level alignment of airborne and ground-based profiles.

The UAV-borne GPR survey was performed at a very low flight altitude of approximately 1 m above ground level (AGL) to maximize electromagnetic coupling between the antenna and the terrain. The platform used was a DJI Matrice 600 Pro multirotor UAV, capable of carrying medium-weight scientific payloads while maintaining stable flight at low altitude. The UAV followed a terrain-adaptive flight path, with altitude continuously adjusted using an integrated GNSS receiver and radar altimeter, ensuring a nearly constant antenna–ground distance throughout the acquisition. Differential corrections were provided via NTRIP from the INGV RING network, using the GROT station located at the Grottaminarda Castle (AV), allowing centimeter-level accuracy in the georeferencing of radar traces.

Mission planning and execution were carried out using UgCS Enterprise v5.9 software, integrated with the Custom Payload (CP) module, which enabled full synchronization between UAV navigation and radar data acquisition. The system was managed through the SkyHub onboard computer, allowing real-time monitoring and control of both flight parameters and sensor operation. The CP module ensured that each radar trace was precisely linked to its spatial position along the track, while the terrain-following functionality dynamically adjusted the UAV altitude based on topographic data, improving the uniformity and quality of the acquired radar profiles.

The GPR system consisted of a Cobra Plug-in Sub-Echo 70 antenna, operating in the 20–140 MHz frequency range, suitable for deep subsurface penetration. The antenna was mounted beneath the UAV using a non-conductive support structure to minimize electromagnetic interference from onboard electronics and was oriented parallel to the flight direction to enhance the detection of sub-horizontal reflectors. The combined configuration allowed continuous data acquisition along the transect at a nominal speed of ~1 m/s. Under these conditions, the system achieved an average depth of investigation of approximately 7.5 m, depending on local subsurface properties.

The first public release includes data from three surveyed sites, selected to represent different environmental and subsurface conditions. Future releases will extend the dataset with additional acquisition campaigns.

The dataset is accompanied by a dedicated GitHub repository providing Python-based tools for data loading, visualization, pre-processing, and baseline experimentation. The codebase supports reproducibility and facilitates further methodological development by the research community.

This resource is intended to support research in geophysics, remote sensing, robotics, signal processing, and machine learning applied to subsurface sensing, particularly in safety-critical and emergency-response scenarios.

 

Data Formats

The dataset is distributed in two standard geophysical data formats to ensure broad interoperability with existing processing tools and research workflows:

  • GeoTable format – This format provides structured tabular storage of GPR traces together with associated metadata (e.g., acquisition parameters, positioning information, timestamps). It facilitates rapid data inspection, custom pre-processing, and integration with scientific computing environments such as Python and MATLAB.

  • SEG-Y (SEGY) format – A widely adopted standard in geophysics for seismic and subsurface data representation. The SEG-Y files contain the raw radar traces along with embedded header information describing acquisition geometry and technical parameters. This format ensures compatibility with professional geophysical software and advanced signal processing toolchains.

Providing both formats enables flexible usage, supporting both traditional geophysical analysis pipelines and modern data-driven approaches.
